text.p: Speciality chemicals group Henkel KGaA on Tuesday posted a 10 percent rise in pre-tax profit to 438 million marks in the first half of 1997, as it reaped the benefits of the weak deutschemark.
Henkel forecast earnings would grow at least as much in the second half.

"The increase is even better than 10 percent because we expected a negative impact from acquiring Loctite ," Henkel's chief financial officer, Ulrich Lehner, said, referring to the U.S.-based adhesives maker.
Group sales in the first six months rose 22 percent to 9.784 billion marks from 8.039 billion. Excluding the Loctite acquisition, sales increased by 13 percent.

The value of Henkel's sales was given a resounding boost by the fact that the mark was much weaker against the dollar during the first six months of this year, lifting the value of Henkel's exports. Seventy percent of the company's sales came from foreign units in the first half.

Henkel said it expected full-year 1997 results to be well above 1996 levels, even without including income from acquisitions, while at the same time including financing costs from what has been a busy period of acquisitions and disposals.
Shares in Henkel responded positively to the interim results and were 3.88 percent higher in mid-session bourse trade, outperforming the overall market.
As well as buying Loctite, the group sold its 16.1 percent stake in chemical group Degussa AG to diversified utility Veba AG.
"The net profit from the sale of our stake in Degussa , because we had to pay some taxes, was about 520 million marks," Lehner said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

The group had said earlier that it had made gross proceeds of around 1.3 billion marks from the disposal of the Degussa stake. The first-half pre-tax profit figure does not include those proceeds. Henkel said it would use the income from the sale to continue strengthening its core activities.
On a turnover basis, the lion's share of growth came from acquisitions.
The biggest rise in terms of the group's individual sectors was in its industrial adhesives/technical consumer products division, where sales in the first half rose 68 percent to 2.086 billion marks.

The group also saw major growth in its surface technologies division, where sales increased by 55 percent to 795 million marks in the first half. Around 39 percent of sales growth came from acquisitions.
In the group's core chemical business, sales grew 14 percent to 2.373 billion marks.
Sales at the group were much higher at the group's foreign units than at its domestic units. Domestic units had sales of 2.281 billion marks, up from 2.264 billion.
Henkel's foreign units saw sales growing to 6.955 billion marks from 5.272 billion marks.
Employee numbers also grew, again mainly through acquisitions, to 52,145 from 46,665.
"There is real growth potential for us now, in eastern Europe and in southeast Asia," Lehner said. Growth would be driven by new products, he said.
